newsitem.title: USA: Republican chances in U.S. Congress races improve.
newsitem.headline: Republican chances in U.S. Congress races improve.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's hopes of a Democratic Congress were fading in the face of a fierce last-minute assault by Republicans intent on keeping their hold on the Senate and House of Representatives.

In the frantic final weekend before the November 5 election, a blizzard of Republican campaign spending on television advertising appeared to be shoring up chances for Republican congressional candidates, political analysts said.

And signs of a narrowing Clinton lead over Republican challenger Bob Dole after allegations of improper Democratic fundraising from foreign sources seemed to reduce the chances Clinton would sweep in a Democratic Congress on his coattails.
Polls showed Senate Republican candidates coming back in state after state as the party poured money in to key races to retain or improve its 53-47 seat advantage.
"At the end of the night, I think Republicans gain one (seat) in the Senate," said Jennifer Duffy, political analyst with the independent Cook Report.

There were far fewer reliable polls in the House, where Republicans hold a 235-197 majority, with two vacancies and an independent who votes with Democrats. Analyst Elizabeth Wilner of the Cook Report doubted Democrats can win the 19 seats from Republicans needed to retake majority control of the chamber.
"I just don't see it," she said of House elections.

She and others caution last-minute polls are not always reliable guides, recalling that not one opinion poll predicted the Republicans would regain control of the House in 1994 for the first time in 40 years.
Nonetheless, the scales seemed to be tipping toward Senate Republicans in some close races.

In the state of Georgia, Republican Guy Millner trailed Democrat Max Cleland by 16 points one month ago in an Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll. This week the same poll showed Millner had pulled slightly ahead, 47 percent to 45 percent.
On Wednesday alone Republicans used a special committee operating without spending limits to buy $321,000 of broadcast airtime for Millner in Georgia, Federal Election Commission reports show.

In the swing state of Oregon, Republican Gordon Smith has held a narrow lead over Democrat Tom Bruggere for weeks. This week it moved to 47 percent to 41 percent in one poll, outside the margin of error for the first time.
Democrats looked to Clinton to give a boost to Bruggere in Oregon, but in the past two weeks Clinton's lead in the state has been cut in half, analysts said.

Republicans also are fighting hard to save vulnerable incumbert Sen. Bob Smith in New Hampshire, who has been in deep trouble from a Democratic challenge by Dick Swett. To boost Smith, Republicans spent $909,315 in recent days to help hold the seat, Federal Election Commission reports show.

Republicans also find reason for encouragement in the House races. Last month Oregon-based independent pollster Tim Hibbitts predicted that Democrats stood to gain two-to-seven seats in the Pacific Northwest region alone.

"Now I think it will be at the lower end of that range," he said. Such candidates as freshman Republican Randy Tate of Washington, virtually written off earlier as a lost cause, is now said to be even with Democratic challenger, Adam Smith.
Tate saved his money for advertising until near the end of the campaign.
